pending_items.title: Israeli opposition advances October 7 attack probe opposed by Netanyahu
pending_items.content:
JERUSALEM, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Israel's opposition-run parliament gave the initial go-ahead on Wednesday for an independent investigation into the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, a probe opposed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu while promised by rivals trying to unseat him.

Wednesday's vote was the first of four needed to pass a law establishing a state commission to investigate Israel's failures in the run-up to the deadliest day in its history.

Parliament also voted in favour of a bill that would impose term limits on prime ministers and restrict them from serving while under criminal indictment, measures apparently aimed at Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, who is facing corruption charges he denies.

Netanyahu remains in office in a caretaker capacity since losing his coalition's parliamentary majority in an election last month.

His opponents have taken control of the agenda in the legislature, although opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot, tapped to form a new government, has so far struggled to cobble together a new ruling coalition to oust him.

Surveys have shown wide public support for a state commission into the country's biggest security lapse in decades.

"For the bereaved families, for the survivors of captivity and those who did not return to us alive, we will uncover the truth and take every step to prevent the next disaster," Eisenkot said in a social media post.

Eisenkot's bloc of Jewish-led opposition parties was joined by parties representing the Arab minority to pass the bill establishing the probe. Some 65 lawmakers voted in favour, while 50 voted against.

Netanyahu opposes an independent probe and has instead demanded a government-empowered inquiry that would grant parliament members authority to pick panel members and the cabinet the power to set its mandate. Critics including Eisenkot describe that as an attempt by Netanyahu to cover up the truth.

There was no immediate comment by Netanyahu or his office. A close Netanyahu ally, Transport Minister Miri Regev, said the "bill will not lead to an examination of the failures that took place," but rather would "investigate our brave, heroic soldiers."

Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages in their attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023. That sparked Israel's military assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and internally displaced nearly the entire population of 2 million.

Netanyahu's coalition of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties lost its parliamentary majority in the October 27 election, reduced to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, though his right-wing Likud party remains the largest party.

Eisenkot's bloc of Jewish-led right-wing, left-wing and centrist lawmakers won just 48 seats. Most of those groups have so far refused to form a coalition with Arab-led parties, which won a record 19 seats. He has until December 6 to form a coalition, with the possibility of a 14-day extension.

So far, Arab lawmakers have voted with Eisenkot and his allies on legislation, allowing them to steer bills through parliament and set its priorities, including electing a member of Eisenkot's Yashar party as Knesset speaker last week.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government, Netanyahu would likely get a shot next. If no government can be formed, new elections would be held.

(Reporting by Emily Rose, Steve Scheer, Lianne Back and Pesha MagidWriting by Rami AyyubEditing by Peter Graff)

pending_items.title: Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib join politicians and legal groups condemning Ulm 5 prosecution
pending_items.content:
Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib are among dozens of politicians and legal organisations raising alarm over the prosecution and treatment of pro- Palestine activists in Germany .

Two letters issued on Wednesday, signed by 26 politicians and 31 legal groups from across the globe, condemned the treatment of five activists who have been held in pretrial detention for over 14 months.

Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Zo Hailu, Crow Tricks, Vi Kovarbasic and Leandra Rollo, who are from Germany, Spain , Ireland and the UK , were arrested on 8 September following an alleged break-in at the premises of Israeli arms firm Elbit Systems in the southwestern German city of Ulm.

Known as the “Ulm Five”, the group is accused of damaging the building's glass facade and smashing office equipment, including computers, screens and telephones.

In addition to charges of trespass and damage to property, the five are accused of "membership of a criminal organisation", namely Palestine Action Germany, under Section 129 of the German penal code.

The legislation is typically used to target organised crime networks and carries a potential sentence of up to five years in prison.

All the defendants have been held in prolonged pretrial detention, where they report facing restrictive conditions.

Under Section 129, suspects can be held for up to six months before trial, though lawyers say this period has now been significantly extended.

In their letter, the elected officials - including members of the German Bundestag, the European Parliament, the US Congress, the Irish Parliament and other legislatures across Europe and the Americas - called for the activists’ “immediate release”.

They further warned that the implications of their prosecution and treatment extend beyond the five defendants, forming “part of an international effort to discipline opposition to war and to place the interests of arms manufacturers above the rights of peoples and the obligations of international law”.

Meanwhile, a separate letter signed by 33 legal groups - including the Center for Constitutional Rights, the Punjab Bar Council, European Democratic Lawyers, the American Association of Jurists, the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, the German Association of Democratic Lawyers - warned that the conduct of the trial could constitute a breach of German and international law.

In particular, the letter raises concerns about the courtroom’s security arrangements, which it said obstruct confidential communication between the defendants and their lawyers and could undermine the presumption of justice.

MEE previously reported that the trial, which began on 27 April, is taking place at a high security courtroom in the notorious Stammheim complex.

The defence team has repeatedly protested their clients’ treatment during proceedings, where the defendants are handcuffed and seated behind a glass barrier, preventing confidential communication with their lawyers.

The legal groups also challenged the court’s rejection of multiple applications by defence lawyers to hear expert witnesses.

MEE previously reported that the court refused to hear weapons expert Dr Shir Hever and international law expert Isabel Feichtner, who were presented by the defence team to give evidence regarding Elbit Systems’ role in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Germany’s obligations under international law.

The organisations further rejected the use of Section 129 against the defendants, insisting that “the prosecution of specific acts of property damage must not be conflated with the criminalisation of a political protest movement”.

"A criminal trial must establish the relevant facts impartially," they urged. "It must not exclude politically inconvenient facts merely because they concern the conduct of a powerful arms manufacturer or the actions of a state in an ongoing armed conflict".

pending_items.title: Israeli lawmakers advance October 7 inquiry opposed by Netanyahu
pending_items.content:
Israel's new parliament on Wednesday took a first step to set up a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas's unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack, a move long opposed by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On the election campaign trail, centrist prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot had pledged to swiftly establish an independent state commission into the failures that allowed Hamas's attack which resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.

Netanyahu, who was in office during the attack and had long billed himself as the guarantor of Israel's security, had rejected calls to set up such a probe which would have broad investigative powers, instead proposing a commission with members appointed by politicians.

In a preliminary reading in the new parliament formed after October 27 elections, 65 members voted in favour of the commission bill put forward by a lawmaker from Eisenkot's party, with 50 against.

The bill will now head to a committee in the Knesset, Israel's parliament, and will have to pass through three further readings before becoming law.

A statement from the Knesset detailing the bill said that the commission would consist of five members and would be required to publish an interim report within one year of the announcement of its establishment.

The bill allocates a budget of seven million shekels (about $2 million) for the commission's creation.

Eisenkot's Yashar party described the legislation as "essential to uncovering the truth and drawing the lessons needed to safeguard Israel's security".

"This is the beginning of a process of setting things right for all Israeli citizens," said Yashar member of parliament Orit Farkash-Hacohen, who submitted the bill.

"We must ensure that what happened on that terrible day never happens again."

Transportation Minister Miri Regev, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, accused the bill's proponents of seeking to target individuals rather than get to the truth.

"They want to investigate our brave and heroic soldiers. They do not want to get to the truth," she said in the Knesset.

Polls have shown broad Israeli support for an independent probe into the deadliest day in the country's history, which inflicted a profound national trauma whose repercussions continue to be felt.

The opposition bloc's legislative offensive follows last week's election of Matan Kahana, a close ally of Eisenkot, as speaker of the Knesset -- a strategic position that allows him to expedite or delay debates and votes on proposed legislation.

In the wake of Kahana's election, a committee responsible for organising parliamentary business decided to fast-track consideration of several bills, exempting them from the usual 45-day waiting period.

Eisenkot intends to take advantage of the accelerated procedure to pass several pieces of legislation before even forming a government.

The former general has vowed to reverse several controversial measures adopted under Netanyahu's government, including a judicial overhaul that sparked one of the largest waves of protests in Israel's history.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu obtained a clear majority in the election. Eisenkot was tapped on November 8 to form a new government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.

Avigdor Liberman, a right-wing ally of Eisenkot, said that a government could be presented by the end of next week.

Liberman has opposed relying on lawmakers from Israeli-Arab parties, which posted unprecedented gains on the back of anger over Netanyahu's government.

The left-leaning Democrats, who support inclusion of the Arab minority, on Tuesday halted talks with Eisenkot, voicing alarm over his negotiations with Netanyahu's Likud Party on a coalition.

But the talks on a unity government have made little apparent progress and some observers saw the Democrats' move as tactical as the party jockeys for influence in the next government.
